title: Jerusalem: A Short History
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: a short history is a dated framework, not a design. Its engineering content is chronological arithmetic — spans between dated events — and the demo computes those spans from the dates the record states, so a reader can check the framework's own arithmetic.
body:
Jerusalem has been inhabited for several thousand years, with settlement on the southeastern hill (the City of David) in the Bronze Age and growth into a walled city in the Iron Age. It served as the capital of the kingdoms of Judah and, in tradition, of united Israel; it was conquered by Babylon in 586 BCE, rebuilt under Persian rule, ruled in turn by Greeks, Hasmoneans, Romans, Byzantines, early Islamic caliphates, Crusaders, Ayyubids, Mamluks, and Ottomans, and became a contested city in the twentieth century. The Old City and its walls were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1981. This record gives that outline as public historical fact, in neutral terms, and leaves detailed period histories to dedicated studies, which the source register lists.

Science proof (chronology): dating in Jerusalem's history rests on written records correlated with archaeological stratigraphy, inscriptions, coins, and radiocarbon dates where organic material survives. A span is the difference of two dates, and the demo computes the spans the record states.

Mathematics: The demo computes spans: from 586 BCE to 1981 CE, from the Babylonian conquest to the Roman destruction of 70 CE, and from 70 CE to 1981 CE.

title: Ancient Jerusalem Geography
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: geography is elevation, slope, watershed, and distance. Ancient Jerusalem sits on a hill system between the Kidron Valley to the east and the Hinnom Valley to the west and south, with the Tyropoeon Valley running through the city, and its water came from the Gihon Spring. Those facts, not any single coordinate, are the record's content.
body:
Ancient Jerusalem occupied a narrow, defensible ridge in the Judean hills, roughly 750 to 800 metres above sea level, with the Mount of Olives across the Kidron Valley to the east rising slightly higher. The original settlement sat on the southern spur above the Gihon Spring, the city's perennial water source, and the city grew northward along the ridge as it expanded. The surrounding terrain is dissected limestone hills, terraced in many periods for agriculture, with rainfall concentrated in winter and a dry summer. That hill-and-valley shape explains the city's walls, which follow ridges and valley edges, and its gates, which open where valleys and roads allow passage.

Science proof: elevation and slope are measured by survey and by digital elevation models, and the valley pattern is visible in any topographic map of the city. The Gihon Spring's flow is a measured hydrological quantity, intermittent in its natural state and managed by tunnels in antiquity.

Mathematics: The demo computes elevation differences: Mount of Olives (about 818 metres) minus the City of David ridge (about 750 metres), and a slope illustration over a 500-metre run.

title: The Old City Walls Through Time
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: a wall is a dated structure with a course, a length, and a height, and each rebuilding reuses or replaces earlier work. The present Old City walls are largely the sixteenth-century Ottoman rebuilding under Suleiman the Magnificent, standing on and beside earlier lines, and the record keeps each phase's wall distinct.
body:
Jerusalem's walls were built, destroyed, and rebuilt many times. The earliest city wall enclosed the City of David spur; Hezekiah's Broad Wall in the late eighth century BCE widened the defended area westward; the Second Temple period wall followed a larger circuit; the Roman destruction of 70 CE left the city unwalled for a time; Byzantine and early Islamic walls followed new lines; and the present walls, about 4.5 kilometres in circuit with 34 towers and 8 gates, were built in the 1530s and 1540s under Suleiman. The record gives that sequence as the public archaeological and historical outline, with the present circuit's figures as the measured modern wall.

Science proof: wall phases are dated by stratigraphy, by pottery sealed under and over wall foundations, by inscriptions, and by masonry style. The present circuit's length is a surveyed measurement, and the demo checks its gate and tower spacing arithmetic.

title: Archaeology of Jerusalem
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: archaeology reads strata — layers of occupation, destruction, fill, and rebuilding — and dates them by the objects sealed within them. A stratum's date is only as good as its sealed finds, and the record states that limit wherever it reports a period.
body:
Excavation in Jerusalem has concentrated on the City of David, the Temple Mount's surrounding areas (without excavation on the Mount itself in recent decades, by agreement and by status), the Jewish Quarter, and the southern wall excavations. Major public findings include the stepped stone structure, the large stone structure debated as a palace, Hezekiah's tunnel and the Siloam inscription, the Broad Wall, Second Temple period streets and shops, and the Byzantine Cardo. Finds are published in excavation reports and held in museums, including the Israel Museum and the Rockefeller Museum. The record reports those findings as public archaeological information, notes where interpretation is debated, and does not settle debates that the published literature has not settled.

Science proof: stratigraphic dating, typological dating of pottery, numismatic dating by coins, and radiocarbon dating of organic samples are the standard methods, and their convergence — not any single method — is what dates a layer. A coin gives a date after which its layer was deposited, not the layer's exact year.

Mathematics: The demo computes a simple stratigraphic count: five layers, each with a sealed-find date, and the earliest possible date for the latest layer.

title: Water Systems of Ancient Jerusalem
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: ancient Jerusalem's water engineering is gravity and rock: springs, pools, channels, and tunnels that move water from the Gihon Spring to where people lived, inside the walls where possible. The engineering content is length, gradient, and discharge, and the demo computes gradient from the tunnel's published figures.
body:
The Gihon Spring, in the Kidron Valley, was the city's water source. Warren's Shaft and earlier channels drew on it; Hezekiah's Tunnel, cut in the late eighth century BCE and about 533 metres long, diverted the spring's water inside the city to the Pool of Siloam, and the Siloam inscription describes the two cutting teams meeting underground. Later systems added the Lower and Upper Aqueducts bringing water from springs south of the city, including around Bethlehem, and a network of cisterns stored rainwater in every period. The record gives those systems as public archaeological fact, with the tunnel's length and the inscription's account stated as published.

Science proof: tunnel gradient is measured by survey: a fall of roughly 30 centimetres over 533 metres gives a gradient of about 0.06 percent, gentle enough to keep water moving without scouring the channel. Discharge estimates follow from channel cross-section and velocity, as in the riverine record.

Mathematics: The demo computes Hezekiah's Tunnel gradient from a 0.3-metre fall over 533 metres, and the walking time through the tunnel at 1 metre per second.

title: The Temple Mount: History and Status, Factual and Neutral
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: the Temple Mount platform is a large artificial platform, roughly rectangular, retaining walls on all sides, with the Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa Mosque standing on it today. Its engineering content is platform area and retaining-wall construction, and the record keeps that content separate from questions of status, which it reports factually.
body:
The platform, known in Jewish tradition as the Temple Mount (Har HaBayit) and in Islamic tradition as the Haram al-Sharif (Noble Sanctuary), is the site of the First and Second Temples in Jewish tradition and of the Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa Mosque, among Islam's holiest sites. Herod the Great greatly expanded the platform in the first century BCE; the Second Temple was destroyed by Rome in 70 CE; the Dome of the Rock was completed in 691-692 CE and Al-Aqsa Mosque in the early eighth century. Since 1967, the site has been administered under the status quo arrangement, with the Jordanian Waqf administering the site and Israel responsible for security, and access rules for visitors and worshippers set under that arrangement. This record states those facts neutrally, from public sources, and makes no claim about sovereignty, rights, or future arrangements beyond the public record.

Science proof: platform dimensions are surveyed (roughly 480 metres by 300 metres at its longest extents, about 14.4 hectares), and the retaining walls' masonry — including the large Herodian ashlars — is documented in archaeological survey. Status facts are documented in public governmental and international sources, cited in the source register.

Mathematics: The demo computes platform area from 480 metres by 300 metres, in square metres and hectares.

Jerusalem has been a pilgrimage destination for Jews, Christians, and Muslims for many centuries, and the public routes are well documented. The ancient pilgrimage festivals brought Jews to the Temple; Christian pilgrimage grew from the fourth century with sites including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre; Islamic pilgrimage includes the Haram al-Sharif. Modern public routes include the Jesus Trail from Nazareth toward the Sea of Galilee and onward connections, the Israel National Trail passing the Jerusalem hills, and the city's own marked walking routes through the Old City and its surroundings. Distances in this record are road and trail distances from public guides, and walking times assume 4 kilometres per hour on level ground, adjusted for hills in the notes.

title: Ancient Units: Stadion
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: the stadion was a Greek unit of length, defined by a racecourse, and its length varied by place and period. No single stadion value is settled for every ancient text, and this record preserves the variants rather than choosing one silently.
body:
The stadion (plural stadia) is the unit behind Revelation 21:16's 12,000 stadia and behind many ancient distance statements. Attested values cluster around 177 to 192 metres: the Olympic stadion about 192 metres, the common Hellenistic stadion about 185 metres, and shorter local stadia near 175 metres. Because the unit varied, any conversion of an ancient stadion figure must state its assumed value, and the famous 2,220-kilometre figure for the New Jerusalem's side is simply 12,000 times 185 metres — an illustration at one assumed value, not a settled measurement. This record states all three values and shows the conversion at each.

Science proof: stadion lengths are established by measuring surviving racecourses (stadia) and by comparing ancient distance statements with surveyed ground distances. The spread of results is the evidence for variation, not a failure of measurement.

Mathematics: The demo converts 12,000 stadia at 175, 185, and 192 metres, giving the side length in kilometres at each assumed value.

title: Ancient Units: Cubit

engineering: Engineering view: the cubit was a body-based unit — forearm length from elbow to fingertip — and its length varied by culture and period. The common cubit is about 44 to 46 centimetres, the royal or long cubit about 52 to 53 centimetres, and the record preserves both, because Revelation 21:17's 144 cubits and Ezekiel's measurements use different traditions.
body:
Cubit standards are attested from Egypt, Mesopotamia, Israel, and Greece, each with its own rod or marked standard. The Hebrew common cubit is usually taken as about 45 centimetres, the Egyptian royal cubit as about 52.5 centimetres, and Ezekiel's long cubit as a common cubit plus a handbreadth (about 52 centimetres). Because the unit is body-based, ancient builders worked from a standard rod rather than from any individual's arm, and modern conversions must name the rod they assume. This record names both common and royal values for every conversion it makes.

Science proof: cubit rods survive in museums, and their lengths cluster at the stated values; building dimensions in cubits, divided by those lengths, match surveyed remains within the expected tolerance of ancient construction. The spread across rods is the evidence for variation.

Mathematics: The demo converts 144 cubits at 45 and 52.5 centimetres, giving the wall height in metres at each assumed value.

title: Jerusalem Climate and Terrain

engineering: Engineering view: climate is measured — monthly rainfall, temperature ranges, and humidity — and terrain is slope and aspect. Jerusalem's climate is Mediterranean: wet winters, dry summers, and the record gives the public averages with their seasonal shape, not a single annual figure alone.
body:
Jerusalem receives roughly 500 to 600 millimetres of rain per year, almost all between November and March, with dry summers from May to September. January averages roughly 9 degrees Celsius, August roughly 25 degrees, with summer days often above 30 and winter nights occasionally near freezing, and rare snow. The terrain — limestone hills dissected by valleys, with terraces holding thin soils — makes runoff fast in winter storms and water storage essential in summer, which is why cisterns and pools appear in every period's archaeology. The record gives those figures as public climatological averages, noting that any single year varies.

Science proof: climate averages come from meteorological station records over decades, and the Mediterranean pattern — winter rain from westerly storms, summer drought under subtropical high pressure — is the standard regional explanation, confirmed by the station data's seasonal shape.

Mathematics: The demo sums a monthly rainfall illustration (twelve months totalling about 550 millimetres) and computes the winter share versus the summer share.

title: Geology Beneath Jerusalem
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: geology is rock units in order, with thickness and character. Jerusalem sits on Cretaceous limestone, dolomite, chalk, and marl, and the building stone of the city — the local limestone known as Jerusalem stone — comes from those units, which is why the city's walls and buildings share a colour.
body:
The Judean hills are built of Cretaceous sedimentary rocks, laid down in ancient seas and later uplifted and folded. The harder limestone and dolomite form ridges and building stone; the softer chalk and marl form slopes and valleys and are quarried for lime. Karst processes — water dissolving limestone — formed caves, including the large Zedekiah's Cave quarry under the Old City, and the Gihon Spring issues where a perched aquifer meets the valley side. Faulting and folding tilt the beds, so a tunnel like Hezekiah's passes through rock of varying hardness, which the Siloam inscription's account of meeting teams reflects in its own way. The record gives that sequence as public geological fact.

Science proof: rock units are mapped by geological survey, dated by fossils and by stratigraphic position, and quarried stone is identified by petrology. Karst dissolution is a measured chemical process: slightly acidic rainwater dissolves calcium carbonate over time.

Mathematics: The demo sums an illustrative stratigraphic column — four units with stated thicknesses — and computes the total section thickness.

title: Jerusalem in Maps: Then and Now
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.

body:
The Madaba Map (sixth century, mosaic) shows Jerusalem schematically with walls, gates, and the Cardo; Crusader maps show the city as a round walled town with the Holy Sepulchre at the centre; Ottoman maps add quarters and gates in surveyed form; the Palestine Exploration Fund's Survey of Western Palestine (1870s-1880s) gave the first modern triangulated maps at 1 inch to the mile. Modern maps use satellite imagery, GPS control, and GIS layers, and the Old City's street pattern — the Cardo line, the Via Dolorosa route, the quarter boundaries — can be traced across all of them. The record gives that sequence as public cartographic history and notes each map's limits: schematic maps are not surveys, and no old map should be read as a modern plan.

Science proof: map scale converts by multiplication — map distance times the scale denominator gives ground distance — and triangulation and GPS control are the standard methods that make modern maps measurable. The demo converts map centimetres to ground metres at three historical scales.

title: Heritage Imaging: Scans and Reconstructions
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: heritage imaging includes photography, photogrammetry, laser scanning, and ground-penetrating radar, each with a resolution and a limit. A scan is a measurement, a reconstruction is an interpretation built on measurements, and the record never presents a reconstruction as if it were a photograph of the past.
body:
Modern Jerusalem heritage work uses laser scanners that record millions of points per structure, photogrammetry that builds three-dimensional models from overlapping photographs, and radar that images shallow subsurface features without digging. Published examples include scans of the Western Wall tunnels, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre's structure, and the Old City's streets, and reconstructions of Second Temple period streets and the Herodian platform in museums and in digital models. Each product states its method and its resolution in its publication, and reconstructions mark restored parts as restored. The record reports those methods as public heritage practice, with the scan-versus-reconstruction distinction kept throughout.

Science proof: laser scanning measures distance by time of flight or phase shift, with millimetre to centimetre accuracy at architectural ranges, and photogrammetry recovers three-dimensional coordinates from parallax between photographs. Ground-penetrating radar's depth and resolution trade off with antenna frequency, a standard physical limit.

Mathematics: The demo computes point counts: a scanner at 1,000 points per square metre over a 500-square-metre facade gives 500,000 points, and file size at 12 bytes per point.

title: Jerusalem's Quarters and Communities, Factual
text_faithful: No faith claim in this record. This record states biology, logistics, or real science only; any faith reading of the same image belongs to the spirituality pair and is not repeated here as science.
engineering: Engineering view: a quarter is a district with boundaries, streets, and institutions, and its description is a matter of public record — names, extents, and the communities that live and worship there — stated without adopting any community's political claim as the record's own.
body:
The Old City is traditionally divided into four quarters — Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Armenian — a division that took its present form in the nineteenth century and remains the standard public description, though communities and institutions overlap its lines in practice. The Muslim Quarter, the largest, holds the Haram al-Sharif and much of the Old City's residential and market life; the Christian Quarter holds the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and Christian institutions; the Jewish Quarter, rebuilt after 1967, holds the Western Wall plaza and synagogues; the Armenian Quarter holds the Armenian Patriarchate and St. James Cathedral. Beyond the walls, modern Jerusalem's neighbourhoods — West and East, Jewish, Arab, and mixed — are described in public demographic and municipal sources, and this record reports their existence and character factually, without demographic claims it cannot source to those publications.

Science proof: quarter boundaries are documented in municipal and historical maps, and community presence is documented in census, institutional, and travel publications. Where sources disagree on a boundary or a figure, the record says so rather than choosing silently.

Mathematics: The demo works the quarter arithmetic from the traditional division: four quarters, one Old City, and the share each quarter represents if the city were divided equally (with the note that the real quarters are not equal in area).

Demo program: the record's demo program is shown on the database page and its exact output is stored as expected_output; the demo was executed at build time.

Status label: established.

def main():
    quarters = ['Muslim', 'Christian', 'Jewish', 'Armenian']
    print(f'quarters: {len(quarters)}')
    for q in quarters:
        print(f'quarter: {q}')
    print(f'equal share illustration: {100 / len(quarters):.0f} percent each (real areas differ)')

main()

quarters: 4
quarter: Muslim
quarter: Christian
quarter: Jewish
quarter: Armenian
equal share illustration: 25 percent each (real areas differ)

body:
This record registers the pair's sources by type. Written histories: standard histories of Jerusalem and of the periods covered, from Bronze Age settlement to the present. Archaeological reports: excavation publications for the City of David, the southern wall, the Jewish Quarter, and the Temple Mount surroundings. Survey and mapping: the Survey of Western Palestine, modern topographic and geological survey maps, and UNESCO's World Heritage listing documents (1981). Climatological and geological data: meteorological station records and geological survey maps of the Judean hills. Status documents: public governmental and international statements on the Temple Mount status quo and on access arrangements. Scriptural citations: short quoted excerpts only, with citation, never whole chapters. Every other record in this pair draws on one or more of these types, and any future correction to a record is recorded here as a register amendment, not as a silent edit.

Science proof: a register's proof is auditability — that any claim in the pair can be followed to a source type and then to a publication. The demo counts the register's source types and the pair's records, and verifies that every record has at least one source type assigned.

Mathematics: The demo counts six source types and sixteen records, and computes sources per record as a coverage illustration.
